title: iPhone 18 Pro Review: The Camera Finally Gets a Variable Aperture
summary:
Apple's newest flagship phones, the iPhone 18 Pro ($1,199) and iPhone 18 Pro Max ($1,299), are here—but there's a twist: there is no regular iPhone 18 this year. Apple is only offering the Pro models, with the base iPhone 18 expected in spring 2027 alongside a mid-tier iPhone 18e. If you've always been happy with the standard iPhone, you should absolutely wait. Don't let the hype machine sway you.

That said, the Pro models are very good phones, even with a $100 price hike over last year. Battery life remains stellar. The Pro Max packs a denser battery; with average use (around 5 hours of screen-on time), the reviewer hovered around 50 percent by the end of the day and easily made it through day two on a single charge. The smaller Pro also comfortably lasted a day with about 40 percent left by bedtime.

The new A20 Pro chip runs every app fluidly and shows a surprisingly sizable leap over the A19 Pro in benchmark tests. It can even run Control, a AAA game from 2019 ported to iOS, though aggressive upscaling makes graphics look grainy and character movements feel a little sluggish. More impressive is Apple's thermal management: the vapor chamber's surface area has been expanded three times, so the phone felt toasty after nearly an hour of gameplay but had no uncomfortable hot spots. This also lets you game longer before thermal throttling kicks in.

The real headline feature is almost invisible—embedded into the main camera. Apple is debuting a variable aperture in the iPhone 18 Pro models. The aperture is the physical opening that lets light reach the camera sensor. A wider aperture lets in more light and has a lower f-stop number, while a narrower aperture restricts light. Most smartphones rely on fixed apertures—the iPhone 17 Pro's main camera, for example, is locked at f/1.78. A variable aperture gives the lens mechanical blades that physically expand or contract in a circular shape. Apple gives you four f-stops: f/1.48, f/1.78, f/2.8, and f/4. Open it to f/1.48 for cleaner low-light shots and faster Night Mode captures, plus real optical bokeh—the soft blurred background effect phone makers have spent years simulating. Step it down to f/4, and the blur recedes, keeping more of the scene in crisp focus. Apple defaults the aperture to "Auto" for people unfamiliar with camera terms.

Other updates include a smaller Dynamic Island that can now show three live activities simultaneously (up from two), and a new burgundy color. The phones come with iOS 27 and the all-new Siri AI, which is infinitely more capable than previous versions, though it still doesn't quite match other AI assistants. If you're coming from an iPhone 17 Pro, 16 Pro, or even a 15 Pro, hold onto your device. But if you're a camera fiend, the variable aperture is a genuine upgrade.
why_it_matters: The review shows a smartphone market splitting in two: premium 'Pro' models get expensive hardware experiments like variable apertures and bigger vapor chambers, while everyone else waits longer and pays more for mid-range phones — a pattern that shapes what features trickle down to affordable devices a few years later.

background_read: Adjustable apertures built from overlapping metal blades — called iris diaphragms — have been standard in film and DSLR lenses for decades, letting photographers control exactly how much light reaches the sensor.

Smartphones dropped them because microscopic moving blades are difficult to build and easy to break, so most phone blur is faked by software: Apple's Portrait Mode, introduced with the iPhone 7 Plus in 2016, used computer processing to imitate background blur rather than real optics.

A few Android handsets have tried mechanical apertures before — Samsung's Galaxy S9 (2018) offered a two-setting 'dual aperture' — but most phone makers stuck with fixed lenses and leaned harder on software processing instead.

The article's other new terms describe hardware with similar logic: the Dynamic Island (the small black pill-shaped cutout at the top of recent iPhones that displays live updates) and the vapor chamber (a flat metal chamber that pulls heat away from the chip) both exist to solve problems software alone cannot.

Control, the 2019 action game by Remedy Entertainment mentioned in the review, was designed for consoles and PCs; fitting a 'AAA' game — a big-budget title from a major studio — onto a phone is a genuine technical stretch that depends on tricks like upscaling, which stretches a lower-resolution image to fill a bigger screen.

perspectives.description: A real mechanical aperture is a genuine engineering step after years of software-faked blur; it gives real optical bokeh, cleaner low-light shots and faster Night Mode. For anyone who shoots constantly, this is a meaningful upgrade rather than a marketing gimmick.

Skipping the regular iPhone 18 pushes buyers toward $1,199+ models or makes them wait months, and the Pro models cost $100 more than last year. Critics see a company using model timing and price tiers to squeeze more money out of loyal customers rather than competing on value.

Computational photography has been so good that hardware changes matter less than they once did: four f-stops are useful, but most users would never notice the difference without being told. This is really the story of hardware and software converging in modern phone cameras.

If variable apertures impress reviewers and buyers, expect the feature to spread to cheaper iPhones and to Android rivals within a couple of years — the same trickle-down happened with multi-lens cameras and OLED screens. The bigger open question is whether Siri's new AI can catch up with competing assistants.
